Module 4 | Algorithmic Trading and Computational Finance¶

Day 3 | Learning Rule-Based Algorithmic Trading by Doing | PREview¶

Hi Team 👋

Below are five questions designed to help you fully grasp the process of building rule-based algorithmic trading strategies—specifically momentum and mean-reversion approaches.

As you work through the five questions, you’ll engage with the full workflow: from defining the problem, collecting and importing data, to wrangling, modeling, visualizing, and reporting. In particular, you’ll gain valuable hands-on experience in detecting trading signals using rule-based learning from data—and then executing algorithmic trading by translating those signals into positions and actionable decisions.

These bite-sized questions will guide you in revisiting key concepts and refining your Python skills for real-world problem-solving and making optimal investment decisions.

*Yay* 😊

Please import historical stock data for the following financial instruments using the Yahoo Finance API, and create a DataFrame containing their closing prices.¶

  • TSLA Stock of Tesla

The timeframe should be set from March 15, 2015, to March 15, 2025 (a span of ten years).¶

Question 1. Please implement a momentum strategy for TSLA.

(1) Use two moving average windows: 22 days and 120 days.¶

(2) The operational definition for translating a signal into a position is as follows:¶

(3) Initiate a buy position when upward momentum is detected (i.e., the 22-day moving average crosses above the 120-day moving average).¶

(4) Continue holding the long position as long as the momentum persists.¶

(5) When momentum is lost (i.e., the 22-day moving average falls below the 120-day), switch to a short-sell position.¶

Finally, visualize your positions using lets-plot to visualize the strategy over time.

Note (For Han):

--> Here its important to inteprete the nuance of the question (i.e operational definition):

  • Buy (1): when upward momentum is detected (SSMA > LSMA)
  • Continue to hold the long position as momentum persists
  • Sell (-1) when momentum is lost (SSMA > LSMA)
  • So essentially only a binary choice: BUY OR SELL

Benchmark against passive following¶

In [13]:
ts_1["passive_following_returns"] =\
(
    np
    .log(ts_1["price"]
         /
         ts_1["price"].shift(1)
        )
)
In [14]:
ts_1["our_strategy_returns"] =\
(
    ts_1["positions"].shift(1)
    *
    ts_1["passive_following_returns"]
)

Question 2. Now, please implement the momentum strategy for TSLA, using the following operational definition for translating momentum signals:

(1) Initiate a buy when momentum is detected.¶

(2) Hold the position when there is no change in momentum.¶

(3) Close (sell) the position when momentum is lost.¶

Note (For Han):

--> Here the operational definition differs a little: (this is where he is adding more flavors to our vanilla version of momentum strategy)

  • Buy (1): when upward momentum is detected (SSMA > LSMA)
  • HOLD (0) when there is no change in momentum
  • Sell (-1) when momentum is lost (SSMA < LSMA)
  • So essentially, there are 3 positions BUY HOLD SELL

(
    np
    .where(BUY_or_SELL["shorter_SMA"] > BUY_or_SELL["longer_SMA"],
           1.0, np.where(BUY_or_SELL["shorter_SMA"] < BUY_or_SELL["longer_SMA"],
                         -1.0,0.0
                        )
          )
)

Question 3. Based on your codes the lead to Answer 1 and Answer 2 above, please assess the following.

Visualization Requirements:¶

  • The y-axis should represent cumulative returns, calculated using simple compounding (i.e., via exponentiation), not log returns.

  • The benchmark (BUY & HOLD) represents the cumulative returns of a passive buy-and-hold strategy.

  • Momentum Strategy A (BUY or SHORT-SELL) reflects the cumulative returns achieved using the algorithmic trading strategy implemented based on the operational definition provided in Question 1.

  • Momentum Strategy B (BUY, HOLD, or SELL) reflects the cumulative returns achieved using the algorithmic trading strategy implemented based on the operational definition provided in Question 2.

To do:¶

  • Compute and compare cumulative returns for both strategies.

  • Visualize the results using lets-plot to create an insightful graphical representation.

(

)

Out[94]:
For TSLA, the passive buy-and-hold strategy substantially outperforms both momentum variants and mean reversion, reflecting the stock’s long-term, trend-dominated growth and high return convexity. The momentum strategies, while capturing portions of upward trends, underperform due to frequent exits triggered by short-term volatility, which leads to missed compounding during extended growth regimes. The introduction of a HOLD state reduces unnecessary trading but does not materially improve performance, as the strategy still interrupts exposure to TSLA’s strongest return periods. 

Mean reversion performs worst, as TSLA does not oscillate around a stable mean; instead, large price deviations often represent persistent regime shifts rather than temporary mispricing. 

Overall, the findings suggest that for assets characterised by strong secular trends and information-driven volatility, continuous market exposure dominates signal-based entry and exit rules, while strategies that trade against trends are structurally disadvantaged. That's why need to diversify LOL...
